title: Ben Graham & the Growth Investor | Hewitt Heiserman | Talks at Google
description:
Hewitt Heiserman authored "It's Earnings That Count" and is finishing his second book, “The Checklist Investor”. He is a member of the Boston Security Analyst Society and CFA Institute. He has written for several investing publications.. He graduated from Kenyon College and received the Faculty Award for Distinguished Achievement. He is an Ironman finisher, and is active in open land preservation.

The slides to pair with this talk can be found at: https://goo.gl/kg1BtL
summary: The speaker argues that investors should focus on the 200-day moving average as a critical trend indicator, noting that stocks falling below this line often experience significant declines. He contrasts this technical approach with value investing principles, citing Ben Graham's net working capital method and Warren Buffett's long-term franchise assessments. The talk also highlights the volatility of specific companies, illustrating how quickly stocks can collapse after breaking key technical levels.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Ben Graham would have bought Google for $48 per share based on his net working capital method.
claims.quote: He gave 100% for your cash. He'd give you a 75% for your receivables. You don't have any inventory. And then he'd subtract all your liabilities. And then he'd take your net working capital, he'd multiply that by 66% of that. And then that would leave you $36 billion. He would pay $36 billion for the business. You've got 745 million shares outstanding, so he'd paid $45. Is that right? $48 for Google.
claims.speaker: HEWITT HEISERMAN

claims.claim: The speaker describes Monster Beverage as the best performing stock of the last 20 years, growing a hypothetical $10,000 into $10 million.
claims.quote: Monster's interesting because this is the best performing stock of the last 20 years. A hypothetical $10000 investment grew to $10 million. We're going to turn this presentation into a book, and I'll have much more to say about Monster in the book.
claims.speaker: HEWITT HEISERMAN

claims.claim: Morningstar estimates Alphabet's intrinsic value at $755 a share while the stock price was $682, representing a 90% price to intrinsic value ratio.
claims.quote: Morningstar-- they do a lot of great work with estimating companies intrinsic value. They project that the business-- Alphabet's worth $755 a share. The stock price as of last week was $682. So the price to intrinsic value is 90%. If you buy Alphabet stock today, you're paying $0.90 cents for a dollar's worth of value.
claims.speaker: HEWITT HEISERMAN

claims.claim: Warren Buffett put 40% of his partnership funds into American Express after the salad oil scandal because he determined its franchise was intact.
claims.quote: It knocked shares of American Express down. Mr. Buffet determined that American Express' franchise was intact, and he put 40% of the partnerships funds into American Express and it then went up five-fold in five years.
claims.speaker: HEWITT HEISERMAN

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Alphabet made $14.4 billion in earnings by 2014, exceeding the $10 billion prediction he made in 2004.
claims.quote: I said that it was unlikely that Google would make $14 billion dollars of earnings by 2014. Actually I said $10 billion. In fact you made $14.4 billion. So congratulations.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker explains that Alphabet invested $8.5 billion in fixed capital last year, which is a use of cash not appearing in the GAAP income statement.
claims.quote: So in Alphabet's case last year you made an investment of $8.5 billion dollars. So that's a $8.5 billion of cash that's coming out of your corporate checking account that does not appear in the GAAP income statement.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Microsoft was a bullish trend for most of the 1990s as the stock price stayed above its 200-day moving average.
claims.quote: Here's Microsoft's stock price versus 200-day moving average during the 1990s. You can see that for most of the time-- most of the time the blue line, the moving average was like a support level.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker states that Microsoft ran into trouble in the 2000s, specifically noting a 50% decline in 2000 after the stock went below its 200-day moving average.
claims.quote: In the 2000s you probably know that Microsoft ran into-- got disoriented. We can see that there was a 50% decline in 2000. This is a 50% decline after Microsoft went under its 200-day moving average.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker points out that Microsoft's stock went down 50% in 2008 after the closing price went below its 200-day moving average during the global credit crisis.
claims.quote: And then in 2008 when we had the global credit crisis. Here again, Microsoft's stock went down 50% after the closing price went below the 200-day moving average.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker indicates that Alphabet is 6% above its 200-day moving average, which is a positive sign if using the 200-day moving average approach.
claims.quote: You're probably asking, what about Alphabet? Well, you're 6% above the 200-day moving average. So this is a positive sign if you're using this approach.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker states that he sold Interactive Brokers after noticing that it went below its 200-day moving average and subsequently fell 24%.
claims.quote: Interactive Brokers is a stock that I own, but I sold after I noticed that it went below its 200-day moving average. And you can see that it then fell 24%.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Deutsche Bank is down 45% and fell below its 200-day moving average, which would have been a sell signal for an owner.
claims.quote: Deutsche Bank is down 45%. It fell below its 200-day moving average. And this an important bank to watch because as Deutsche Bank goes, I think Europe will go too.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker highlights that Horsehead Holding is down 99.48% in less than one year, illustrating how violently companies can collapse.
claims.quote: Horsehead Holding is down 99.48% in less than one year. Look how violently some of these companies can collapse.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker states that Linn Energy is down 99% since it went below its 200-day moving average, noting it fell 50% to $14 and then continued to fall.
claims.quote: Linn Energy, down 99% since it went below its 200-day moving average. Now, probably some of you are math majors. So check this out. After Linn went below its 200-day moving average it fell 50% to $14.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker mentions a Vanguard index fund for the corporate bond market where the daily closing price is $22.68 and the 200-day moving average is $22.50 to $22.60.
claims.quote: This is a Vanguard index fund. And then the average of the last 200 days of closing prices is $22.50-- $22.60. So on this basis, Paul Tudor Jones-- I don't want to put words in his mouth, but my interpretation is he would be bullish on corporate bonds.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker notes that for Vanguard's total stock market index fund, the 200-day moving average is $50.60 while Friday's close was $45.92, meaning the market is in bear territory.
claims.quote: This is Vanguard's total stock market index fund. The 200-day moving average is $50.60. And then Friday's close was $45.92. So this means we're in bear territory.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman
